gloss: A device held in the hand and used to do a particular job.
examples: Every *tool* in the garage has its own hook on the wall.
You'll need a few basic *tools* to put this together.
A screwdriver is the one *tool* I use almost every day.

gloss: Metal parts such as screws, hinges, and handles, sold for building and repair.
examples: The cabinet comes with all the *hardware* you need.
I picked up some *hardware* on the way home.
Don't lose the *hardware* — those screws are hard to match.

gloss: A box with a handle for carrying and storing tools.
examples: His *toolbox* weighs a ton.
There's a flashlight in the bottom of the *toolbox*.
Both *toolboxes* were sitting open on the tailgate.

gloss: A set of tools or parts packaged together for one purpose.
examples: I keep a small repair *kit* under the seat.
The shelf came as a *kit* with all the screws included.
They sell first-aid *kits* right by the register.

gloss: A tool with a heavy metal head used to drive nails or strike things.
examples: Hand me the *hammer* — this nail is bent.
He hit his thumb with the *hammer* and yelled.
The store had a whole wall of *hammers*.

gloss: A tool with a shaped tip for turning screws.
examples: Do you have a flathead *screwdriver*?
I fixed the outlet cover with a *screwdriver* in two minutes.
Half my *screwdrivers* are missing again.

gloss: A tool with jaws or a shaped opening for turning nuts and bolts.
examples: Tighten that bolt with a *wrench*, not pliers.
He kept an adjustable *wrench* in the truck.
The set came with twelve *wrenches* in different sizes.
contrast: The w is silent: RENCH. The British call this tool a spanner.

gloss: A tool with a toothed blade for cutting wood, metal, or stone.
examples: This *saw* is too dull to cut anything.
He cut the board in half with a hand *saw*.
The shop had *saws* hanging along the back wall.
contrast: Sounds exactly like saw, the past tense of see.

gloss: A saw with a fine blade held in a frame, used for cutting metal.
examples: A *hacksaw* will go right through that bolt.
I broke two blades on the *hacksaw*.
Both *hacksaws* need new blades.

gloss: A power saw whose teeth run around a moving chain.
examples: He cleared the fallen tree with a *chainsaw*.
Don't start the *chainsaw* without safety glasses.
After the storm you could hear *chainsaws* all over the neighborhood.

gloss: A tool that spins a pointed bit to make holes.
examples: Can I borrow your *drill* for an hour?
The battery on my cordless *drill* is dead.
They keep the *drills* locked in the back.

gloss: The removable cutting piece that a drill turns to make a hole.
examples: You need a smaller *drill bit* for that screw.
The *drill bit* snapped off inside the wall.
I bought a set of *drill bits* on sale.

gloss: The flat cutting part of a knife, saw, or similar tool.
examples: Change the *blade* before you cut the tile.
The *blade* on this saw is chipped.
Razor *blades* are behind the counter.

gloss: A tool with a flat sharpened end, struck to cut wood or stone.
examples: He shaped the joint with a *chisel* and a hammer.
Keep the *chisel* sharp or it will tear the wood.
A set of wood *chisels* makes a good gift.

gloss: A metal hand tool with a rough surface for smoothing metal or wood.
examples: Run a *file* over that edge so it doesn't cut you.
He smoothed the weld with a flat *file*.
The metal *files* are in the second drawer.

gloss: A large heavy hammer swung with both hands.
examples: It took a *sledgehammer* to break up the old steps.
Don't swing that *sledgehammer* near the window.
The rental yard had *sledgehammers* by the door.

gloss: A heavy iron bar with a flattened end, used to pry things apart.
examples: Use a *crowbar* to pull those old boards off.
He pried the lid open with a *crowbar*.
There were two *crowbars* in the back of the truck.

gloss: A tool with a heavy blade on a handle, used for chopping wood.
examples: He split the firewood with an *ax*.
The *ax* is hanging in the shed.
Both *axes* needed sharpening.
contrast: Americans write ax or axe; the British write only axe. The plural axes is AK-siz — the plural of axis is AK-seez.

gloss: A device that squeezes two things together and holds them.
examples: Put a *clamp* on the joint while the glue dries.
The *clamp* left a mark in the wood.
I need two more *clamps* for this.

gloss: A heavy clamp fixed to a bench that grips a workpiece.
examples: He held the pipe in a *vise* while he cut it.
Every workbench should have a *vise* bolted to it.
The shop had *vises* on all four benches.
contrast: Americans spell it vise, the British vice. Either way it sounds like vice.

gloss: A hollow metal cap that fits over a nut or bolt head and turns on a handle.
examples: Grab the half-inch *socket* for that nut.
The *socket* wouldn't fit over the bolt head.
Half the *sockets* are missing from the set.

gloss: A pointed metal fastener with a spiral ridge, turned into place.
examples: This *screw* keeps stripping.
Use a shorter *screw* so it doesn't go through.
The kit came with sixteen *screws*.

gloss: A thin pointed piece of metal hammered in to hold things together.
examples: Drive the *nail* in at an angle.
There's a *nail* sticking out of that board.
He bought a five-pound box of *nails*.

gloss: A thick metal pin with a head and a thread, fastened with a nut.
examples: Tighten the *bolt* until it's snug.
One *bolt* had rusted solid.
Four *bolts* hold the seat to the floor.

gloss: A small metal block with a threaded hole that screws onto a bolt.
examples: The *nut* came loose and the whole thing wobbled.
Hold the *nut* with pliers while you turn the bolt.
Don't overtighten those *nuts*.

gloss: A flat ring placed under a nut or bolt to spread the pressure.
examples: Put a *washer* under the bolt head.
The faucet was leaking because of a worn *washer*.
The bag had a hundred *washers* in it.

gloss: A metal pin hammered flat at both ends to join two pieces permanently.
examples: A *rivet* holds the handle to the blade.
One *rivet* popped and the bracket came loose.
The old bridge is held together with *rivets*.

gloss: A short U-shaped piece of wire driven in to hold something down.
examples: The wire is held down with a *staple*.
He drove a *staple* right through the cable.
Use fence *staples* to hold the wire to the post.

gloss: A tool that drives staples into paper or into a surface.
examples: The *stapler* is out of staples.
He used a heavy-duty *stapler* on the insulation.
There are two *staplers* in the supply closet.

gloss: A short thin rod that holds two parts together or in line.
examples: A small *pin* holds the hinge together.
The *pin* sheared off under load.
Take the *pins* out before you fold it.

gloss: A sleeve pushed into a wall so a screw can grip where there is no wood.
examples: Use a drywall *anchor* if there's no stud.
The *anchor* pulled right out of the plaster.
The mirror came with four *anchors* and screws.
contrast: The ch is a hard k: ANG-kur.

gloss: Any small part such as a screw, bolt, or nail that holds things together.
examples: Any *fastener* will work as long as it's stainless.
Keep every *fastener* in a labeled bag.
The store has a whole aisle of *fasteners*.
contrast: The t is silent, as in fasten and listen: FAS-uh-nur.

gloss: An angled support fixed to a wall to carry a shelf or fixture.
examples: The shelf sits on two metal *brackets*.
One *bracket* was bent, so the shelf sagged.
Screw the *bracket* into a stud.

gloss: A jointed metal fitting that lets a door or lid swing open.
examples: The *hinge* squeaks every time you open it.
One *hinge* had pulled out of the frame.
Oil the *hinges* and the noise will stop.

gloss: A simple catch that holds a door, gate, or lid closed.
examples: The gate *latch* is stuck again.
Lift the *latch* and push.
Both *latches* on the toolbox are broken.

gloss: A curved piece of metal for hanging or catching something.
examples: Hang the ladder on that *hook*.
The *hook* pulled out of the wall.
There are coat *hooks* by the back door.

gloss: A small springy fitting that grips something and holds it in place.
examples: A plastic *clip* holds the wire in place.
The *clip* snapped when I pulled too hard.
Those *clips* keep the hose from sliding off.

gloss: A coil of metal that pushes back when you press or stretch it.
examples: The *spring* in the screen door is worn out.
A broken *spring* is why the gate won't close.
Garage door *springs* are dangerous to replace.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A toothed wheel that turns another one; also equipment for an activity.
examples: One *gear* inside the drill was stripped.
Bring your own safety *gear* to the job site.
The *gears* grind if you shift too fast.
contrast: A toothed wheel is countable (two gears); equipment is uncountable (a lot of gear, never 'gears').

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: The spiral ridge that runs around a screw or bolt.
examples: The *thread* on this bolt is stripped.
Clean the *threads* before you screw it back in.
Wrap the *thread* with tape so the joint doesn't leak.

gloss: A block that is thick at one end and thin at the other, driven in to split or hold.
examples: Drive a *wedge* into the crack to split the log.
He used a *wedge* to hold the door open.
A couple of *wedges* will level that post.

gloss: A device that keeps a door or lid shut until it is opened with a key.
examples: The *lock* on the shed is rusted shut.
Change the *lock* before you move in.
All the *locks* take the same key.

gloss: A detachable lock with a U-shaped bar that passes through a hasp or chain.
examples: There's a *padlock* on the gate.
I cut the *padlock* off with a hacksaw.
Both *padlocks* use the same combination.

gloss: A shaped piece of metal that opens a lock.
examples: I lost the *key* to the toolbox.
The *key* doesn't turn all the way.
He had six *keys* on the ring.

gloss: A rounded handle you grip and turn.
examples: The door *knob* came off in my hand.
Turn the *knob* all the way to the right.
The cabinet *knobs* are brass.
contrast: The k is silent: NAHB.

gloss: The part of a tool or door made to be held.
examples: The *handle* on the hammer is cracked.
Grab it by the *handle*, not the blade.
Both drawer *handles* were loose.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A line of connected metal rings used to pull, hold, or secure something.
examples: Put a *chain* through the gate and lock it.
The bike *chain* came off again.
They sell *chain* by the foot at the hardware store.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Thick cord made by twisting fibers together.
examples: Tie the ladder down with a *rope*.
The *rope* frayed where it rubbed the edge.
They sell *rope* by the foot.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A thin flexible strand of metal, often used to carry electricity.
examples: A loose *wire* was causing the short.
Run the *wire* along the baseboard.
Twist the two *wires* together and cap them.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A thick wire or bundle of wires inside a protective covering.
examples: The *cable* runs under the floor.
We pulled two hundred feet of *cable* through the attic.
Label both *cables* before you unplug them.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A flexible insulated wire that carries power to an appliance.
examples: The *cord* on the vacuum is too short.
Don't yank the *cord* out of the wall.
Tape the *cords* down so nobody trips.
contrast: Sounds exactly like chord, a group of musical notes.

gloss: A length of flexible cord that carries power farther from an outlet.
examples: Run an *extension cord* out to the driveway.
That *extension cord* isn't rated for outdoor use.
We needed two *extension cords* to reach the shed.
contrast: American extension cord; the British say extension lead.

gloss: The pronged end of a cord that fits into an electrical outlet.
examples: The *plug* doesn't fit that outlet.
One prong on the *plug* is bent.
Check the *plugs* before you blame the breaker.

gloss: The point in a wall where a plug is inserted to get electricity.
examples: There's an *outlet* behind the couch.
That *outlet* stopped working last week.
The kitchen has *outlets* every four feet.
contrast: American outlet; the British say socket or power point.

gloss: A small lever or button that turns an electric current on and off.
examples: The light *switch* is on the wrong wall.
Flip the *switch* and see if it comes on.
Both *switches* control the same light.

gloss: A safety part that melts and breaks a circuit when the current is too high.
examples: A blown *fuse* killed the whole circuit.
Replace the *fuse* with the same rating.
Older houses have *fuses* instead of breakers.

gloss: The glass part of a lamp that gives off light.
examples: The *bulb* burned out again.
Let the *bulb* cool before you touch it.
I bought a four-pack of LED *bulbs*.

gloss: A sealed unit that stores electricity and powers a device.
examples: The *battery* in the drill won't hold a charge.
Swap the *battery* and try again.
Keep spare *batteries* in the drawer.

gloss: A device that puts power back into a battery.
examples: The *charger* takes about an hour.
I left the *charger* at the job site.
Both *chargers* fit the same battery.

gloss: A rigid tube that carries water, gas, or air.
examples: A *pipe* burst under the sink.
Cut the *pipe* an inch shorter.
The copper *pipes* were green with corrosion.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A flexible tube that carries water or air.
examples: The garden *hose* is kinked.
Screw the *hose* onto the spigot.
Both *hoses* leak at the coupling.

gloss: The narrow end fitted to a hose or sprayer to shape the stream.
examples: Put the *nozzle* on the end of the hose.
The *nozzle* was clogged with dried paint.
The sprayer came with three *nozzles*.

gloss: A fitting that opens and closes to control the flow in a pipe.
examples: Shut the *valve* before you cut the line.
The *valve* under the sink is corroded.
There are shutoff *valves* on both sides.

gloss: The fitting you turn to let water out of a pipe.
examples: The kitchen *faucet* drips all night.
He replaced the *faucet* in about an hour.
Both bathroom *faucets* need new washers.
contrast: American faucet; the British say tap.

gloss: A machine that moves liquid or air from one place to another.
examples: The sump *pump* runs every time it rains.
The *pump* burned out after ten years.
They keep two *pumps* in the basement.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A narrow strip with glue on one side, used to stick or seal things.
examples: Wrap the joint with plumber's *tape*.
Hand me the roll of *tape*.
I keep three kinds of *tape* in the drawer.

gloss: Strong cloth-backed sticky tape used for quick repairs.
examples: He fixed the mirror with *duct tape*.
There's a roll of *duct tape* in the truck.
He wrapped the handle in *duct tape*.

gloss: A sticky substance used to join two surfaces.
examples: Put a little *glue* on both edges.
The *glue* hasn't dried yet.
Wood *glue* is stronger than the wood itself.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A substance made to bond materials together.
examples: This *adhesive* works on metal and plastic.
Spread the *adhesive* evenly before you set the tile.
They carry industrial *adhesives* in the back.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Colored liquid spread on a surface to color and protect it.
examples: The *paint* is still tacky.
One more coat of *paint* should do it.
They mixed two *paints* to match the old color.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A clear coating brushed on wood to give it a hard shiny surface.
examples: Put a coat of *varnish* on the tabletop.
The *varnish* yellowed over the years.
Marine *varnishes* hold up better outdoors.

gloss: A soft paste that hardens, used to fill holes and set glass.
examples: Fill the nail holes with *putty*.
The *putty* has to dry before you sand it.
He smoothed the *putty* with his thumb.

gloss: A flexible filler squeezed into seams to keep water and air out.
examples: Run a bead of *caulk* along the tub.
The old *caulk* was black with mildew.
Let the *caulk* cure overnight.
contrast: The l is silent — caulk rhymes with talk.

gloss: A soft metal melted to join two pieces of metal or wire.
examples: Heat the joint before you apply the *solder*.
The *solder* didn't flow into the seam.
Use lead-free *solder* on water lines.
contrast: Americans drop the l: SAH-dur, not SOL-dur.

gloss: Thick oily material put on moving parts to reduce friction.
examples: Pack the wheel hub with *grease*.
There was *grease* all over his hands.
A little *grease* will stop that squeak.

gloss: Stiff paper coated with grit, rubbed on a surface to smooth it.
examples: Smooth the edge with fine *sandpaper*.
I'm out of *sandpaper*.
Wrap the *sandpaper* around a block of wood.

gloss: A power tool that smooths a surface with moving sandpaper.
examples: The belt *sander* took the finish off fast.
Wear a mask when you run the *sander*.
Both *sanders* need new pads.

gloss: A power tool with a spinning wheel that cuts or smooths metal.
examples: He cut the bolt off with an angle *grinder*.
Sparks flew everywhere from the *grinder*.
The shop has two bench *grinders*.

gloss: A power tool with a spinning bit that cuts grooves and shaped edges in wood.
examples: He rounded the edge with a *router*.
The *router* left burn marks in the oak.
Both *routers* take the same bits.
contrast: In America it rhymes with out: ROW-tur. The British say ROO-tur.

gloss: A machine that burns fuel to make electricity.
examples: We ran the fridge off a *generator* for three days.
The *generator* is loud but reliable.
Portable *generators* sold out before the storm.

gloss: A machine that turns electricity or fuel into movement.
examples: The *motor* on the fan is burned out.
You can hear the *motor* struggling.
Small electric *motors* are cheap to replace.

gloss: A powered device with moving parts that does a particular kind of work.
examples: This *machine* hasn't been serviced in years.
Shut the *machine* off before you clean it.
The shop is full of old *machines*.
contrast: The ch sounds like sh: muh-SHEEN.

gloss: A piece of equipment made for a specific purpose.
examples: It's a simple *device* with one moving part.
Every safety *device* on the saw had been removed.
These *devices* measure moisture inside a wall.

gloss: A sturdy table where tools are used and things are built.
examples: He built a *workbench* out of scrap lumber.
Clear the *workbench* before you start.
Both *workbenches* have a vise on the end.

gloss: A room or building where things are made and repaired with tools.
examples: His *workshop* is out behind the garage.
The *workshop* smells like sawdust.
They rent *workshops* to local woodworkers.

gloss: A building beside or under a house where a car and tools are kept.
examples: The car doesn't even fit in the *garage* anymore.
He keeps all his tools in the *garage*.
Most of the houses have two-car *garages*.
contrast: Americans stress the second syllable, guh-RAHZH; the British stress the first, GA-rij.

gloss: A small simple building used for storing tools and equipment.
examples: The mower lives in the *shed*.
The roof of the *shed* leaks.
They put up two *sheds* in the back yard.

gloss: A frame of rungs between two side pieces, used for climbing.
examples: Hold the *ladder* while I go up.
The *ladder* only reaches the second floor.
Extension *ladders* are heavier than they look.

gloss: A folding ladder with flat steps that stands on its own.
examples: Grab the *stepladder* from the garage.
Don't stand on the top step of a *stepladder*.
Both *stepladders* are aluminum.

gloss: An open container with a handle, used for carrying liquids or materials.
examples: Fill the *bucket* with warm water.
He carried the paint in a five-gallon *bucket*.
Stack the empty *buckets* by the door.

gloss: A tool with bristles on a handle, used to paint, sweep, or scrub.
examples: Clean the *brush* right after you paint.
Use a stiff *brush* on the rust.
Cheap *brushes* leave bristles in the paint.

gloss: A covered cylinder on a handle, rolled over a surface to spread paint.
examples: A *roller* covers a wall much faster than a brush.
Load the *roller* evenly.
The *rollers* are in the paint aisle.

gloss: A rubber cup on a stick used to push a blockage through a drain.
examples: Every apartment needs a *plunger*.
He cleared the drain with a *plunger*.
There are *plungers* in the cleaning closet.

gloss: A tool with a broad blade and a long handle for digging and lifting.
examples: Grab a *shovel* and start digging.
The *shovel* handle snapped.
Both *shovels* are in the truck bed.

gloss: A long-handled tool with teeth, used to gather leaves or level soil.
examples: I need a *rake* for all these leaves.
The *rake* lost half its teeth.
Garden *rakes* are on sale this week.

gloss: A small open cart with one wheel and two handles for moving loads.
examples: Load the dirt into the *wheelbarrow*.
The *wheelbarrow* has a flat tire.
They had two *wheelbarrows* going all afternoon.

gloss: A flexible marked strip that rolls into a case, used to measure length.
examples: Where's the *tape measure*?
The *tape measure* snapped back and got my finger.
I own four *tape measures* and can never find one.

gloss: A straight strip marked with units, used to measure and draw lines.
examples: Draw the line against a *ruler*.
A metal *ruler* works better than plastic.
The *rulers* are in the desk drawer.

gloss: A tool with a bubble in liquid that shows whether a surface is flat or upright.
examples: Set the *level* on top of the shelf.
The bubble in the *level* is off center.
Laser *levels* have gotten cheap.

gloss: An instrument that shows a measurement such as pressure or thickness.
examples: Check the tire pressure with a *gauge*.
The *gauge* reads sixty pounds.
Both *gauges* were stuck at zero.
contrast: Spelled g-a-u-g-e but said GAYJ, rhyming with page.

gloss: A machine that spins a piece of wood or metal while a tool shapes it.
examples: He turned the table leg on a *lathe*.
The *lathe* in the shop is older than I am.
Metal *lathes* take up a lot of floor space.
contrast: The th is voiced — lathe rhymes with bathe, not with path.

gloss: A tool that burns gas in a hot flame for soldering, welding, or heating.
examples: He heated the pipe with a *torch* before soldering it.
Keep the *torch* away from anything flammable.
The plumber carried two *torches* in his kit.
contrast: In America a torch makes a flame; in Britain a torch is what Americans call a flashlight.

gloss: A small battery-powered lamp you carry in your hand.
examples: Bring a *flashlight* — there's no light down there.
The *flashlight* batteries are dead.
We keep *flashlights* in every room.
contrast: American flashlight; the British say torch.

gloss: A device that lifts a heavy object a short distance off the ground.
examples: Put the *jack* under the frame, not the body panel.
The *jack* slipped and the car dropped.
Both *jacks* are rated for two tons.

gloss: A grooved wheel that a rope or belt runs over to lift or drive something.
examples: A *pulley* makes the load feel half as heavy.
The rope came off the *pulley*.
The system runs on two *pulleys* and a cable.
contrast: The first syllable sounds like pull: PUUL-ee, not PYOO-lee.

gloss: A bar that turns on a fixed point to move a heavy load with less force.
examples: Use a long bar as a *lever* and it'll move.
The *lever* on the side releases the blade.
There are two *levers* under the seat.
contrast: Americans usually say LEV-ur; the British say LEE-vur.

gloss: A temporary frame of poles and planks that workers stand on.
examples: They put up a *scaffold* along the whole wall.
Don't climb the *scaffold* without a harness.
The *scaffolds* came down after the siding was finished.
contrast: The second syllable is reduced: SKAF-uld, not skaf-FOLD.

gloss: Wood that has been sawn into boards for building.
examples: The *lumber* is stacked behind the shed.
The price of *lumber* went up again.
We need enough *lumber* for a twelve-foot deck.
contrast: American lumber; the British say timber. Uncountable — never 'a lumber' or 'lumbers'.

gloss: Board made of thin layers of wood glued together.
examples: Cover the window with a sheet of *plywood*.
The floor is just *plywood* for now.
Half-inch *plywood* should be strong enough.

gloss: Panels of plaster in paper, used to finish interior walls.
examples: They hung the *drywall* in one afternoon.
There's a hole in the *drywall* behind the door.
Cutting *drywall* makes an unbelievable mess.
contrast: American drywall; the British say plasterboard. Uncountable.

gloss: A long thick flat piece of sawn wood.
examples: One *plank* on the deck is rotting.
He walked out on a *plank* laid across the joists.
The *planks* were warped from the rain.

gloss: A long heavy piece of wood or metal that supports a structure.
examples: A steel *beam* carries the whole second floor.
The *beam* over the doorway is original.
The old barn has hand-hewn *beams*.

gloss: One of the upright posts inside a wall frame.
examples: Find a *stud* before you hang that.
The screw missed the *stud* completely.
The *studs* are sixteen inches apart.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A hard block of baked clay used for building.
examples: One *brick* worked loose from the chimney.
The house is built of *brick*.
They hauled the *bricks* in by hand.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A flat piece of baked clay or stone used to cover a floor, wall, or roof.
examples: One *tile* cracked when he dropped a wrench.
The bathroom floor is *tile*.
We still have a box of spare *tiles*.

gloss: A gray powder that hardens when mixed with water, used to bind concrete.
examples: Mix the *cement* with sand and water.
A bag of *cement* weighs about ninety pounds.
The *cement* set faster than we expected.
contrast: Stressed on the second syllable: suh-MENT.

gloss: A hard building material made from cement, sand, gravel, and water.
examples: They poured the *concrete* on Tuesday.
The *concrete* cracked along the seam.
You can't drive on the *concrete* for three days.

gloss: A straight slender bar of metal or wood.
examples: A threaded *rod* holds the two halves together.
The *rod* bent under the weight.
Cut the *rods* to length before you install them.

gloss: A hard strong metal made from iron and carbon.
examples: The frame is welded *steel*.
Bare *steel* rusts if you don't paint it.
Stainless *steel* costs more but lasts.
contrast: Sounds exactly like steal, to take something that isn't yours.

gloss: A knife with a short sliding blade, used to open cartons.
examples: Open the carton with a *box cutter*.
The blade on the *box cutter* is dull.
They handed out *box cutters* on the loading dock.
